blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the **new head**. Every arrow should point the other way.

blocks.alt: Before: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null. After: 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null. The same nodes, with every arrow flipped.

elements.text: the head becomes the tail, and the tail becomes the new head
elements.originalText: the head becomes the tail, and the tail becomes the new head

blocks.code:
Input:  head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Input:  head = [1, 2]
Output: [2, 1]

Input:  head = []
Output: []

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: copy the values out, write them back reversed
Don't touch the arrows at all. Walk the list once to copy every value into an array, then walk it again and write the values back **from the end of the array**.

blocks.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    values = []
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        curr.val = values.pop()   # last value first
        curr = curr.next
    return head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** It gives the right output, but it cheats: the nodes never move, only their values. An interviewer will usually ask you to reverse the **links**, and to do it without an O(n) copy.
2. Optimal: recursion — reverse the rest, then fix one arrow

Trust recursion with the hard part. If the list is `1 → (2 → 3 → 4 → 5)`, first reverse everything **after** the head. That gives `5 → 4 → 3 → 2`, and node 2 — still `head.next` — is now its tail. So just hang the head behind it: `head.next.next = head`, and make the head the new tail: `head.next = null`.

blocks.alt: Recursion on 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. The call on 2..5 returns 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> null with new head 5. Then node 2's next is set to node 1, and node 1's next is set to null.
blocks.caption: Each call fixes exactly one arrow on its way back up.

elements.text: head.next = null        (1 is the new tail)
elements.originalText: head.next = null        (1 is the new tail)

blocks.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:   # 0 or 1 node: already reversed
        return head
    new_head = reverse_list(head.next)      # reverse everything after head
    head.next.next = head    # the node after head now points back to it
    head.next = None         # head becomes the tail
    return new_head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** It really relinks the nodes — but every call waits on the call stack until the end of the list is reached. With 100,000 nodes that's 100,000 stack frames, enough to crash with a stack overflow in many languages.
3. Best solution: flip the arrows in one pass (three pointers)

Walk the list once and flip each arrow as you pass it. You need three pointers: `prev` (the part already reversed), `curr` (the node being flipped) and `next` (a bookmark, so the rest of the list isn't lost when `curr.next` changes).

blocks.alt: Halfway through: null <- 1 <- 2 are already flipped, prev points at 2, curr at 3, and next at 4. 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null are still in the original direction. A note lists the four moves: save next, flip curr.next to prev, move prev to curr, move curr to next.
blocks.caption: Save, flip, step, step — repeated until curr falls off the end. Then prev is the new head.

elements.text:
next = curr.next     // 1. bookmark the rest
curr.next = prev     // 2. flip the arrow
prev = curr          // 3. step prev forward
curr = next          // 4. step curr forward
elements.originalText:
next = curr.next     // 1. bookmark the rest
curr.next = prev     // 2. flip the arrow
prev = curr          // 3. step prev forward
curr = next          // 4. step curr forward

blocks.caption: Watch the arrows flip one at a time. The bookmark `next` is what keeps the rest of the list reachable.

blocks.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr is not None:
        nxt = curr.next     # 1. bookmark the rest
        curr.next = prev    # 2. flip the arrow
        prev = curr         # 3. step prev forward
        curr = nxt          # 4. step curr forward
    return prev             # the old tail is the new head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** One pass, three pointers, no recursion and no copy.

rows.timeWhy: One pass to copy, one to **write back**.

blocks.text: All three are linear. The brute force only swaps values and needs a full copy; the recursion relinks properly but uses a call stack as deep as the list; the iterative version relinks with three pointers and nothing else.

items: **Empty list** — `[]` returns `[]`; the loop never runs and `prev` is null.
**Two nodes** — `[1, 2]` returns `[2, 1]`: the smallest case where an arrow actually flips.

blocks.text: Reversing is a building block: **Palindrome Linked List** and **Reorder List** later in this chapter both reverse the second half of a list as one of their steps.
